title: Forces and Newton's Laws of Motion

State Newton's three laws of motion and explain the cause and effect relationship each one describes.
Choose a system of interest and identify the external forces acting on it.
Use F_net = ma to determine the acceleration of a system.
Explain why forces occur in pairs and why action and reaction act on different bodies.
Distinguish mass from weight, and inertia from force.

sections.title: Introduction to Dynamics: Newton's Laws of Motion
sections.locator: CNXML module m42129, Introduction to Dynamics: Newton’s Laws of Motion
objectives: Describe what dynamics studies and why forces are the subject of it.
Explain the role observation played in the development of Newton's laws.
State the conditions under which Newton's laws of motion give a good approximation.

misconceptions.claim: Newton's laws describe motion exactly, at any speed.
misconceptions.correction: The laws are an approximation. They hold well for objects moving at speeds much less than the speed of light, and only in an inertial frame of reference.
misconceptions.locator: CNXML module m42129, paragraph on the limits of the laws

misconceptions.claim: Galileo established the laws of motion by reasoning alone.
misconceptions.correction: Galileo made observation, not logical argument, the determinant of truth, and his telescope work was the most notable example of that shift.
misconceptions.locator: CNXML module m42129, paragraph on Galileo

summary: Dynamics is the study of the forces that cause objects and systems to move.
Newton's laws mark the transition from the Renaissance to the modern era.
Observation, not argument, was the determinant of truth in the development of the laws.
The laws are a good approximation at speeds far below the speed of light.
sections.no_worked_example_reason: This section is the historical introduction and the source carries no worked example for it.

sections.title: The force concept and the free-body diagram
sections.locator: CNXML module m42069, Development of Force Concept
objectives: Define force as a vector quantity with magnitude and direction.
Draw and read a free-body diagram for a body in a given situation.
Explain how a stretched spring can serve as a standard of force.

misconceptions.claim: A body can exert a force on itself.
misconceptions.correction: A body cannot exert a force on itself. The hawk that accelerates while gliding is pushed by the air and pulled by the Earth, not by itself.
misconceptions.locator: CNXML module m42069, conceptual question on the hawk

misconceptions.claim: The action and the reaction in Newton's third law cancel each other out.
misconceptions.correction: They do not cancel, because they act on two different bodies. The swimmer pushes on the wall and the wall pushes on the swimmer.
misconceptions.locator: CNXML module m42069, paragraph on the swimmer

summary: A force has magnitude and direction, so it is a vector.
A free-body diagram shows only the external forces acting on one body.
Force can be measured against a standard, such as the pull of a stretched spring.
A body never exerts a force on itself.

statement.text: Two skaters push on a third skater, as in the figure. Which forces appear in the free-body diagram of the third skater?

steps.expression: The figure shows two skaters pushing the third with forces $F_1$ and $F_2$.
A free-body diagram shows only the external forces acting on the body, with the body represented by a single isolated point.
The forces the third skater receives from the other two are external to it, so both appear.
The forces between the two pushers are internal to the pair of pushers and do not appear in the third skater's diagram.

answer.text: $F_1$ and $F_2$, the two external pushes, and nothing else from the other skaters.

sections.title: Inertia and Newton's first law
sections.locator: CNXML module m42130, Newton’s First Law of Motion: Inertia
objectives: State Newton's first law of motion.
Define inertia and relate it to mass.
Explain why a net external force is required for any change in velocity.

misconceptions.claim: An object in motion continues at constant speed only if no force acts on it at all.
misconceptions.correction: It is the net external force that matters. A book sliding across a table keeps moving for a while because friction, a net force, is small.
misconceptions.locator: CNXML module m42130, paragraph on the sliding object

misconceptions.claim: Mass and weight are the same thing.
misconceptions.correction: Mass is an intrinsic property of a body. Weight is the gravitational force on that body, so it changes with the gravitational field.
misconceptions.locator: CNXML module m42130, conceptual question on mass and weight

summary: A body at rest stays at rest, and a body in motion stays in motion at constant velocity, unless a net external force acts.
Inertia is the tendency of a body to resist change in velocity.
Mass measures inertia.
Cause and effect: a net external force is the cause of every change in motion.

statement.text: A book slides across a rough table and stops. Which force caused the change in its velocity?

steps.expression: Newton's first law says a body in motion remains in motion at constant velocity unless a net external force acts.
The book slowed down, so its velocity changed, so a net external force acted on it.
The only force acting along the table is friction from the rough surface.
Spraying the surface with talcum powder reduces friction, and the book then slides much further, which is the same cause with a smaller size.

answer.text: The net external force of friction from the rough surface.

provenance.title: College Physics 2e
provenance.locator: CNXML module m42130, paragraph on the object sliding along a rough horizontal surface

sections.title: Newton's second law and the choice of system
sections.locator: CNXML module m42073, Newton’s Second Law of Motion: Concept of a System
objectives: State Newton's second law and define net external force.
Choose a system of interest and identify which forces are external to it.
Use F_net = ma to predict acceleration for a given system and net force.

misconceptions.claim: Acceleration is proportional to the net force and to the mass.
misconceptions.correction: Acceleration is directly proportional to the net external force and inversely proportional to the mass.
misconceptions.locator: CNXML module m42073, paragraph on inverse proportionality to mass

misconceptions.claim: Any force on a system counts towards its net external force.
misconceptions.correction: Only forces acting from outside the system are external. Internal forces between the parts of the system cancel.
misconceptions.locator: CNXML module m42073, paragraph on external forces

summary: A change in motion is a change in velocity, which is an acceleration.
Net external force is the vector sum of all external forces on the system.
Acceleration is directly proportional to net external force and inversely proportional to mass.
F_net = ma

hints: Work out the thrust from the mass and the acceleration, then remember that the friction force does not change.
Use Newton's third law: the force on the ground equals the force on the person.

sections.title: Newton's third law and symmetry in forces
sections.locator: CNXML module m42074, Newton’s Third Law of Motion: Symmetry in Forces
objectives: State Newton's third law of motion.
Explain why forces occur in pairs and why action and reaction act on different bodies.
Apply the third law to everyday situations such as swimming, walking and rowing.

misconceptions.claim: The action and reaction forces on a body balance each other, so nothing can move.
misconceptions.correction: They act on two different bodies, so they never cancel on the same body. That is exactly why the swimmer accelerates away from the wall.
misconceptions.locator: CNXML module m42074, paragraph on the swimmer and the wall

misconceptions.claim: The force that moves a boat forward comes from the rower's arms.
misconceptions.correction: It comes from the interaction between the oars and the water. The rower's arms supply the push on the oars, not the force on the boat.
misconceptions.locator: CNXML module m42074, conceptual question on rowing

summary: Forces always occur in pairs.
A body cannot exert a force on another without experiencing a force itself.
Action and reaction act on two different bodies.
The third law explains swimming, walking, rowing and a hawk gliding.

hints: Write F = ma first, then divide the net force by the acceleration.
Choose the system that includes both skaters, then apply the third law to the push between them.

exam_traps.subject: physics
exam_traps.misconception: The same force for the same time gives the massive body the higher velocity.
exam_traps.correction: The two bodies gain the same impulse, so their momenta are equal. The lighter body moves faster.
exam_traps.signal: The paper offers the higher velocity for the massive body as an option, and the answer is that the momenta are the same.

exam_traps.subject: physics
exam_traps.misconception: A body moving at constant velocity needs a force to keep it moving.
exam_traps.correction: Newton's first law says a body in motion stays in motion at constant velocity unless a net external force acts. The net force on it is zero.
exam_traps.signal: The paper offers a force greater than the friction as the answer, and the answer is that the resultant force is zero.

exam_traps.subject: physics
exam_traps.misconception: A body can exert a force on itself.
exam_traps.correction: It cannot. A hawk that accelerates while gliding is pushed by the air and pulled by the Earth.
exam_traps.signal: Our own question offers the body as its own source of force.

exam_traps.subject: physics
exam_traps.misconception: The action and the reaction cancel, so nothing can move.
exam_traps.correction: They act on two different bodies, so they never cancel on one body. That is why the swimmer accelerates away from the wall.
exam_traps.signal: Our own question offers the cancellation as an option.

exam_recall_checks.subject: physics
exam_recall_checks.stem: A net force of 12 N acts on a body of mass 3 kg. What is the acceleration of the body?
exam_recall_checks.explanation: Newton's second law gives a = F/m = 12/3 = 4 m/s².
exam_recall_checks.source: authored against the JAMB physics syllabus

exam_recall_checks.subject: physics
exam_recall_checks.stem: A swimmer pushes against the wall of a pool with a force of 200 N. What force does the wall exert on the swimmer?
exam_recall_checks.explanation: The forces are equal in magnitude and opposite in direction. They act on two different bodies, so they do not cancel.
exam_recall_checks.source: authored against the WAEC physics syllabus

exam_recall_checks.subject: physics
exam_recall_checks.stem: Which of the following is a contact force?
exam_recall_checks.explanation: Friction acts between surfaces that touch. The other three act at a distance.
exam_recall_checks.source: authored against the JAMB physics syllabus

equal in magnitude to the weight of the book
